title: Introduction: The Status Quo of Multi-Format Media Publishing
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 119, Issue: 1, 2010)

authors.bio: Al Kovalick has worked in the field of file-based workflows for the past 16 years. Previously, he was a digital systems designer and technical strategist for Hewlett-Packard. He was the principal architect of HP's first VOD server. Following HP, from 1999 to 2004, he was the CTO of the Broadcast Products Division at Pinnacle Systems. Currently, he is with Avid Technology and serves as a Strategist and Fellow. Kovalick contributes to SMPTE activities including standards development and is a frequent member of the Technical Conference program committee, and a presenter at SMPTE regional seminars. He received the David Sarnoff Gold Medal in 2009. Kovalick is an active speaker, educator, and author. He has presented more than 50 papers at industry conferences worldwide. He holds 18 US and foreign patents and is the author of the 512-page book Video Systems in an IT Environment (2009). He has a BSEE degree from San Jose State University and MSEE degree from the University of California at Berkeley. He is a member of the IEEE, a SMPTE Fellow, life member of Tau Beta Pi, and a member of the Board of Directors of the Advanced Media Workflow Association. On December 2, 1992 John Malone, CEO of the largest cable operator in the U.S. at the time, famously predicted 1 that digital compression would expand his modest 50-channel analog system to a 500 channel universe. He was correct of course. However, looking back, maybe he should have said 500K “channels” or more. That is what we have today, in effect, with the “any content, anywhere, anytime, any device” 2 consumption mantra. This is fueled by increased access to content via networks of all sorts.

authors.bio: Curtis Clark's credits include such artful narrative films as The Draughtsman's Contract, Dominick and Eugene, Alamo Bay, Extremities , and Talent for the Game. His extensive commercial cinematography projects have put him on the cutting edge, working for some of the industry's top directors and agencies. Clark currently heads the American Society of Cinematographers (ASC) Technology Committee, which examines and addresses imaging technology issues as they relate to the creation of motion pictures and cinematography. That committee worked closely with Digital Cinema Initiatives (DCI) to produce the ASC-DCI Standard Evaluation Material (StEM) used to evaluate the performance of digital projectors and other elements of digital cinema systems.

authors.bio: Clyde D. Smith is Senior Vice President of Global Broadcast Technology and Standards for Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. In this capacity, Smith is responsible for the strategic development and planning of new technology, standards and technical practices development, adoption and implementation, to support the Domestic and International News and Entertainment Groups. Previously, as supervisor of Communications Design and Development Engineering for Lockheed Space Operations Company at The Kennedy Space Center, Smith participated in the design team that implemented NASA's improvements of space shuttle transportation systems, following the Challenger accident. Smith held a key role in creating the technology that resulted in Turner Broadcasting System, Inc., being awarded a 2003 Emmy for Outstanding Achievement in Technology and Engineering for “Pioneering Efforts in the Development of Automated, Server-Based Closed Captioning Systems.” In 2006, he received Broadcasting and Cable's Technology Leadership Award. He is a recipient of the SMPTE outstanding service award and the SMPTE Progress Medal recognizing his outstanding technical contributions to the progress of engineering phases of the television industry. At the 2008 Consumer Electronics Show, he received the Storage Visions Conference's “Storage Industry Service Award”. A SMPTE Fellow, Smith has served as Governor, Standards Chair, Secretary/Treasurer, and program chair for four SMPTE Advanced Motion Imaging conferences.

authors.bio: Gary Demos is the recipient of the 2005 Gordon E. Sawyer Oscar for lifetime technical achievement from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. He was a pioneer in the development of computer- generated images for use in motion pictures, and in digital film scanning and recording. He was a founder of Digital Productions (1982–1986), Whitney-Demos Productions (1986–1988), and DemoGraFX (1988–2003). He is currently involved in digital motion picture camera technology and digital moving image compression. Demos is currently senior algorithm scientist for Lowry Digital. He is also CEO and founder of Image Essence LLC, which is developing wide-dynamic-range codec technology based upon a combination of wavelets, optimal filters, and flowfields.

title: A 3-D Journey into Digital Intermediate (DI): Setting the Stage
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 117, Issue: 7, October 2008)

authors.bio: Christopher Townsend graduated with a graphic design B.A. honors degree in England in 1988. He spent the next six years traveling and working in various countries, including China, Australia, New Zealand and Singapore. He specialized in graphic design and animation for broadcasting and television advertising, before moving to the U.S. to work on feature films at George Lucas' esteemed Industrial Light and Magic. Over the next 11 years, he worked as an artist and supervisor on some of the most influential visual effects movies of our time, including the rerelease of the original Star Wars: A New Hope , as well as the last three films in the trilogy; Mission: Impossible; The Lost World: Jurassic Park; Al: Artificial Intelligence; Hulk; Day After Tomorrow; The Island; The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, The Witch and The Wardrobe and the Academy Award winning Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man's Chest. He was the visual effects supervisor on Journey to the Center of the Earth , the Walden/New Line feature film that was theatrically released in Summer 2008, and directed by Academy Award winner Eric Brevig. More recently, Townsend has been supervising on location for Fox's Wolverine.

title: Producing Quality 3-D Films in the Digital Intermediate Process: Filmmaking
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 117, Issue: 7, October 2008)

authors.bio: Steve Schklair , founder and CEO of 3ality Digital Systems, has been working at the front edge of new technologies for most of his career. He has left a mark in movies, special effects, and in interactive media. Schklair is currently focused on the development and production of new digital 3-D motion picture technologies and the real-time broadcast of 3-D programming. He is highly esteemed by an international client list as one of the world's leading experts in digital and live action 3-D and is one of the primary catalysts behind the recent resurgence of 3-D in Hollywood films. Schklair served as 3-D and Digital Image Producer on 3ality Digital's U23D movie. In addition to supervising the production, Schklair also oversaw the post-production and completion at the 3ality Digital studio in Burbank. Prior to 3ality, Schklair was a senior executive at Digital Domain, the special effects studio responsible for films such as Apollo 13, The Fifth Element, Titanic , and Terminator 2:3D , creative director for R/Greenberg Associates, and he was executive producer for computer graphics and interactive media pioneer Robert Abel. Schklair has a number of new patents pending and is a frequent speaker on 3-D and new entertainment technologies at leading international digital and entertainment technology events. He is a member of the advanced Technology Committee at the American Society of Cinematographers (ASC) and is an alumnus of the Master's program at the University of Southern California's School of Cinema.

authors.bio: Rob Engle is senior stereographer and digital effects supervisor at Sony Pictures Imageworks, where he is currently working on the stereoscopic version of the film G-Force. Prior to G-Force, Engle served as stereographer and 3-D digital effects supervisor on Robert Zemeckis' Beowulf. In that capacity he was responsible for all creative and technical aspects of adapting the film for its release in digital and IMAX 3-D theaters. Preceding his work on Beowulf 3-D, Engle supervised Monster House 3-D, Open Season: An Imax 3-D Experience and the breakthrough release of Zemeckis' The Polar Express: An Imax 3-D Experience among numerous other films. As recent interest in 3-D cinema has peaked, Engle's artistic and technical expertise have made him a highly sought-after speaker at industry events. He is a member of the Visual Effects Society (VES) Board of Directors and co-chair of the VES Archives Committee. He holds a Master of Science degree in computer science from Stanford University and a Bachelor of Science degree in electrical and computer engineering from the University of Colorado.
authors.name: Rob Engle

authors.bio: Buzz Hays is senior producer of 3-D stereoscopic feature films at Imageworks, where he is responsible for overseeing the adaptation of standard release feature films into three-dimensional stereoscopic versions for the IMAX 3-D and digital 3-D platforms. He is one of the leading experts in the field of modern stereoscopic film production. Most recently, he produced the 3-D version of Robert Zemeckis' Beowulf. Hays' work also includes producing the 3-D version of the Imagemotion performance-capture film Monster House , as well as the first CG feature from Sony Pictures Animation, Open Season. Prior to joining Imageworks, Hays worked for Radium where he executive produced visual effects for numerous music videos and broadcast commercials worldwide. Hays holds a Master of Fine Arts in Film Production from the University of Southern California and a Bachelor of Science in Theatre Lighting and Scenic Design from the University of Maine. He is a member of the Producer's Guild of America and the Visual Effects Society.

authors.bio: Jean-Pierre Vitton has a Ph.D. in electronics and optics of materials and a B.S. in chemistry. He has worked at Eastman Kodak Co. for over 19 years. During his ten years in the Corporate Research Lab, he has written more than 20 papers on international research reviews. He is now responsible for sound at the entertainment imaging division of Kodak at “Centre de Technologie Photographique” in France. He was responsible for technical characterizations of Improved Kodak Panchromatic Sound Recording Film 2374. Vitton is a member of SMPTE.
authors.name: Jean-Pierre Vitton

authors.affiliation: Senior engineer at the Eastman Kodak Co., Rochester, NY.
authors.bio: Steven M. Gerlach is a senior engineer at the Eastman Kodak Co., Rochester, NY. He has worked in a variety of divisions at Kodak for over 20 years. He is currently involved with optimizing the manufacture of ECN and black-and-white motion picture films in Rochester. His interests are in design for manufactura-bility and he works closely with the research division as new technologies are developed, then transferred to manufacturing. In 2001, Gerlach received an Academy Award for Science Technology for his work in developing the Panchromatic Sound Recording Film 2374, introduced in 1995.
authors.name: Steven M. Gerlach

authors.bio: Marian Herz left Kodak in 2004 to become director, product line marketing for a Speciality Pulp business at Weyerhaeuser Corp. in Seattle, WA. Prior to that she worked at Kodak for more than 24 years, most recently as product marketing manager in the company's entertainment imaging division where she was responsible for managing black-and-white motion picture film products, motion picture chemicals, and various other film and digital products. During her tenure at Kodak, Herz also held positions as business analyst in the entertainment imaging division, manager of new product development, associate trade marketing manager, sales account executive, and business research analyst in Kodak's U.S. consumer imaging division. Prior to Kodak, Herz worked for several years as an executive manager in a not-for-profit agency. She also owns her own fine art photography business. Herz has an MBA in finance from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor; and a B.A. degree from Smith College in Northampton, MA.
authors.name: Marian Herz

authors.bio: Susan D. Hill has worked at Kodak for over 25 years. She has a B.S. in chemical engineering with graduate-level studies in computer software and business administration. She has led R&D teams in bringing new chemistries to Vision Color Print film and bring black-and-white motion picture print film and sound films to the marketplace. Hill is currently on the Kodak R&D administrative team, responsible for leading the media R&D productivity initiative, directed at workflow re-design across Kodak's media product lines.

authors.name: L. Czúni

authors.bio: Attila Hanis obtained an M.Sc. degree in information technology from the University of Veszprém in 1998. Currently, he is a research fellow at the University of Veszprém and is working on his Ph.D. dissertation. His research interests are video segmentation and video indexing.
authors.name: A. Hanis

authors.bio: Levente Kovács has been working towards a Ph.D. degree in image processing at the University of Veszprém, Hungary, since 2002. His current research interests include non-photorealistic stroke-based image-rendering techniques and image restoration methods. He received an M.Sc. degree in information technology from the University of Veszprém in 2002, and a B.Sc. in electrical engineering in 2004.
authors.name: L. Kovács

authors.bio: Balázs Kránicz is an assistant professor at the Colour and Multimedia Laboratory, University of Veszprém, Hungary. He graduated (same university) in 1997 with an M.Sc. in informatics. He defended his doctoral theses in 2002. Kránicz's research fields are interpolation methods for spectral measurements, deconvolution procedures, spectral fitting of optical detectors by filter packages, determining spectral sensitivity functions, and colorimetric characteristics of computer peripheries, daylight simulators.
authors.name: B. Kránicz

authors.bio: Attila Licsár received an M.Sc. degree in computer science from the University of Veszprém in 2001. Presently, he is a Ph.D. student in the field of image processing in the department of image processing and neurocomputing of the same university. His major research interests involve human-computer interaction, gesture analysis, and digital film restoration, including correction of image vibration and flickering.
authors.name: A. Licsár

authors.bio: Tamás Szirányi received a Ph.D. degree in electronics and computer engineering in 1991, and a Ph.D. degree in image processing in 2001 from the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. Until 1991, he was a research fellow and head of the opto-electronics R&D department at the Videoton Development Institute, Budapest. At the time, his work involved designing optical data storage, laser printer, and document scanning devices, and also applications of laser systems. Szirányi is currently a scientific advisor at the Computer and Automation Research Institute of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. He is also a full professor in the image processing and neurocomputing department of Veszprém University. He is the founder and past-president (1997–2002) of the Hungarian Image Processing and Pattern Recognition Society (KÉPAF) and was honored with the Master Professor award in 2001.
authors.name: T. Szirányi

authors.bio: Iván Kas started his career on CAD/CAM systems in the field of electronics at the Computer and Automation Research Institute (SZTAKI) of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. At SZTAKI, he developed automatic testing equipment based on novel measurement principles and algorithms. His doctoral thesis (1981) was based on this topic. Later his interest was focused on intelligent peripheries and laser technology as he participated in the development of various industrial instruments. He developed his skills in the management of several medium-scale development projects and coordinated software development and various domestic R&D projects. Kas has written 28 papers and owns 16 patents. He has been awarded several scientific and industrial prizes.
authors.name: I. Kas

authors.bio: György L. Kovács graduated, received a Ph.D. degree in habilitation, and became a professor at the Technical University of Budapest, in 1966, 1976, and 1995 respectively. In 1997, he became Dr. of the Academy at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. Since 1966, he has worked in the Computer and Automation Institute. Kovács has been head of the CIM Research Laboratory since 1990. He has been a visiting researcher in the U.S., Soviet Union, West Germany, and a visiting professor in Mexico and Italy. He has more than 250 scientific publications.
authors.name: G. Kovács

Currently, he is head of the Infocomunication Center of this institute.

title: New Methods of Image Capture to Support Advanced Post-Production
label: SMPTE Motion Imaging Journal ( Volume: 113, Issue: 5-6, 2004)

authors.bio: Graham Thomas joined the BBC Research & Development department in the U.K. in 1983 after graduating from Oxford University with an honors degree in Physics. He was awarded a Ph.D. from the University of Essex in 1990 for research in motion estimation. Most of his recent work has focused on techniques for virtual studio production, including the development of the award-winning free-d camera tracking system. Thomas currently leads a team of engineers who are developing a range of production technology based on 3-D graphics and image processing. He recently led Prometheus, a U.K. government-funded R&D project to develop an object-based 3-DTV system. He is the (co) inventor of over 20 patents and has published many papers on image processing for broadcast applications.
authors.name: G. A. Thomas

authors.bio: Michael Koppetz is a senior engineer with the R&D department of Arnold & Richter (ARRI). He graduated from the Technical University of Munich in 1986 with a mechanical engineering degree and joined ARRI in the same year. In the course of his career, he took on the responsibility of the optical and mechanical design group at ARRI's Munich facility and was project leader for several new camera products. With the general reorientation of ARRI's R&D activities, Koppetz moved the focus of his work away from the traditional products and today is intensively involved in the company's development of digital camera technologies, contributing expertise based on his background in the design of professional film cameras.
authors.name: M. Koppetz

authors.bio: Oliver Grau received a master's degree in electrical engineering and a Ph.D., both from the University of Hanover, Germany, in 1991 and 1999, respectively. From 1991 to 2000 he worked as a research scientist at the University of Hanover and was involved in several industrial, national, and international projects in the field of industrial image processing and 3-D scene reconstruction for computer graphics applications. In April 2000, he joined the BBC Research & Development department as a senior research engineer in the virtual production team. His main interest is in visual engineering, i.e., the application of image processing, computer vision, and computer graphics for the production of visual media. Grau was also organizer of the 1st European Conference on Visual Media Production, in March 2004.
authors.name: O. Grau

title: Opportunities for Migrating IP Distribution into Station Workflow

authors.affiliation: Pathfire, Inc. (formerly Video Networks, Inc.), Roswell, GA.
authors.bio: Joe Fabiano is chief technical officer, Pathfire, Inc. (formerly Video Networks, Inc.), Roswell, GA. A founding member of the Pathfire leadership team, Leonard (Joe) Fabiano has more than 19 years of experience in broadcasting and cable as well as electronic video systems expertise. He led the development of Pathfire's innovative, store and forward news distribution and management system, News Tracker, which has been used by NBC News Channel to distribute their network feed to affiliate stations. Following this success, the team developed Pathfire's next generation platform, Digital Media Gateway (DMG), which is used by ABC News One to deliver their network feed to stations. In addition to news, the DMG enables the digital distribution and management of multiple types of content including syndication, short form, and ads. Prior to his entrepreneurial success, Fabiano provided insight, direction, and industry expertise to Cox Communications, serving as corporate director of operations. At Texscan, he was national service manager, creating and implementing automation for the cable advertising sales process.
authors.name: Joe Fabiano

authors.affiliation: Broadcast, for Pathfire, Inc. (Formerly Video Networks Inc.), Roswell, GA.
authors.bio: Floyd Christofferson is senior vice-president, broadcast, for Pathfire, Inc. (formerly Video Networks Inc.), Roswell, GA. After college Birkmaier held a number of positions in commercial broadcast facilities where he learned the production and operations side of the television industry. In 1979 he joined Industrial Sciences. Inc. in Gainesville, Fla., handling inside sales, order processing, and expediting Many orders involved custom design capabilties, requiring extensive coordination between the customer and the engineering staff. This work led to the development of many standard ISI products including the 904 Video Production Switcher, and the 831 and 899 Master Control Switchers. In 1981 he joined the Grass Valley Group, where he established a channel of distribution and created new products and promotion programs. In 1985, he joined Intergroup Video Systems where he implemented a marketing plan that required a restructuring of the professional video dealer organization: the recruitment and training of a National Sales Manager, three regional sales managers, and an inside sales specialist: the development of internal systems for lead tracking, direct mail, order entry, and sales analysis HE also guided a promotional campaign which introduced the new corporate identity, and provided a sustaining product advertising and a direct mail program. In 1986, Birkmaier formed Professional Products & Promotion (P') a marketing, consultancy which provided marketing and promotional services to manufacturers and distributors of television communications products. Later in 1986, reacting to need in the industry for a broader range of consulting services to augment the internal products. development capabilities of manufacturers. Birkmaier, together with several experienced video design engineers, formed ProTech Designs, Inc. ProTech and P' offer the ability to conceive a product, develop a business plan and product proposal, and then work with a manufacturer to market the product.

He joined the London-based Designs Department of the British Broadcasting Corporation in 1961 and worked there on the development of a range of studio color equipment until 1966. In 1966 Thorpe left the BBC to join the Broadcast Division of RCA in Camden, New Jersey, where he remained until 1982. In 1975 he became project leader of the TK-47 automatic color camera, for which he received a David Sarnoff award in 1981. In 1982 Thorpe resigned from RCA to join the new Sony Broadcast Company where he was Director of Studio Product Management. authors.affiliation: National Broadcasting Company New York, N.Y.
authors.bio: Dr. Kerns H. Powers retired from RCA in 1987, after 35 year of service, with a speciality of communications engineering, especially television. He is currently a consultant for NBC, the David Sarnoff Research Center, and other clients. After graduation from the University of Texas in 1951, Dr. Powers joined RCA Laboratories at Princeton, New Jersey, to work on dot sequential television, the forerunner of NTSC. Over the years at RCA, his work involved high-resolution radar, ELF transmission, data communication, satellite communication, video, and enhanced definition television. He became a group head in 1959. Director of the Communications Research Laboratory in 1966, and Staff Vice-President, Communications Research in 1977. At the time of his retirement, he was in charge of research in support of the communications, broadcasting, and government systems businesses of RCA. Dr. Powers received B.S.E.E. and M.S.E.E. degree from the University of Texas in 1951, and an Sc.D. from Massachusetts Institute of Techology in 1956. He has 16 issued patents and has published numerous technical papers. His honors include the Forty-One for Freedom from the U.S. Navy in 1967, delivery of the prestigeous Shoenberg Lecture before the Royal Television Society in 1987, and the Progress Medal of SMPTE in 1988. He is a Fellow of the IEEE and of SMPTE.

authors.bio: Peter Centen holds B.S and M.S degrees and a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from Eindhoven University of Technology, The Netherlands. As a researcher at Philips Research Laboratories, he worked on optimal signal processing for CCD-imagers, noise reduction of CCD-imager output circuitry, and its highspeed operation. Implementation of this work resulted in the LDK-HS series. For many years he has been involved in the development of HDTV cameras and switchable SDTV cameras at the R&D department of Thomson multimedia Broadcast Solutions, formerly known as Philips DVS. At present he is a group leader in the camera R&D department of Thomson, responsible for the implementation of CCDs in professional video cameras and the front-end design of the multiformat HDTV camera head. As a co-inventor, Centen holds patents for Dynamic Pixel Management (DPM) and HD-DPM, and is founder of the optical filtering method using DPM. He is a member of the IEEE and has published numerous journal and conference articles.

authors.bio: Dave Bancroft is business and technology development manager for the Film Imaging Group of Philips Digital Video Systems. Although his group is based in Weiterstadt, Germany, Bancroft operates out of the U.K. and contributes to long-term projects, such as DTV production, in the U.S. Bancroft began his career in broadcast engineering at the BBC in London, where he received his fundamental training and became an operations and maintenance engineer on outside broadcasts. He became particularly interested in videotape recording and related mechanical wonders and this led to an international odyssey, which kept him away from the U.K. for 20 years. During this time, he worked for RCA in Germany, Ampex Corp. in Greece, the Middle East, Africa, New York, and California. He joined Philips Digital Video Systems, or as it was formerly known, BTS, in 1992, with the assignment of HDTV marketing in Darmstadt. He moved his desk back to the U.K. in 1995 and took up his present position with Philips in 1997. Bancroft is a long-time member of SMPTE, where he represents Philips in several technology committees. He is an International Member of SMPTE's Executive Standards Committee. title: On Scanning Format and MPEG-2 Coding Efficiency
label: SMPTE Journal ( Volume: 110, Issue: 5, May 2001)

authors.affiliation: Philips Research Laboratories in Briarcliff, NY
authors.bio: Erwin Bellers received his B.S. degree in computer engineering from the Technische Hogeschool, in Enschede, and his M.S. degree in electrical engineering from the University of Twente, in 1987 and 1993, respectively. He received his Ph.D. degree from the Delft University of Technology in 2000 with his thesis about de-interlacing. In 1993, Bellers joined Philips Research Laboratories in Eindhoven as a research scientist in the Video Processing and Visual Perception Group. In 2000, he moved to Philips Research USA as a senior scientist. He was a member of several video processing projects, and focused his research mainly on algorithms and the corresponding (hardware) architecture. His major interest is in video enhancement algorithms, particularly motion-compensated de-interlacing, motion estimation, motion-compensated picture-rate upconversion, and resolution enhancement. His work has resulted in two books on de-interlacing, 15 patents and patent applications, and 20 published papers. Bellers is a member of the IEEE.
authors.name: E. B. Bellers

authors.affiliation: Philips Research Laboratories, Eindhoven, The Netherlands
authors.bio: Gerard de Haan received B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. degrees from Delft University of Technology in 1977, 1979 and 1992, respectively. In 1979, he joined the Philips Research Laboratories in Eindhoven, where he led research projects in the area of video processing, and participated in European projects. He has coached students from various universities, and since 1998, teaches at the Philips Centre for Technical Training. Presently, he is a Research Fellow in the Video Processing and Visual Perception Group of Philips Research, and a part-time professor at the Eindhoven University of Technology. De Haan has a particular interest in algorithms for motion estimation, scan rate conversion, and image enhancement. His work in these areas has resulted in some 55 papers, more than 50 patents and patent applications, and several commercially available ICs. He is a senior member of the IEEE.

title: Evolution of Resolution in Film Scanners
label: SMPTE Journal ( Volume: 110, Issue: 12, December 2001)

authors.affiliation: Cintel International, Ware, Hertfordshire, U.K.
authors.bio: Peter R. Swinson has been associated with Cintel for nearly 20 years. He joined Rank Cintel Ltd. in 1982 as telecine products manager responsible for development of the URSA family of telecines and the Klone 4K CCD scanner. Presently, at Cintel International, he is director of market development, involved in the introduction and evolution of C-Reality and Rascal film scanners. A firm believer in the future of film as an acquisition material, Swinson has had several patents issued in his name, mainly involved with novel methods of film scanning and film recording. His current interests are D-cinema and full film resolution scanning as a one stop digital archive.

title: Implementing Digital Television in Australia

authors.affiliation: TX Australia, Chatswood, New South Wales, Australia
authors.bio: Bob Greeney is the engineering manager of TX Australia, directly responsible for the implementation and operation of analog and digital television transmitters for the commercial television networks and for some of the ABC and SBS television services in each capital city. authors.bio: Wolfgang Ruppel holds a professorship for Media Technology at RheinMain University of Applied Sciences, Wiesbaden. His current research areas include stereoscopic 3D, digital cinema and post-production and mastering formats. Before joining RheinMain University, Ruppel worked for more than 10 years in various R&D units within Deutsche Telekom group. As head of Development Digital Cinema, he was responsible for the architecture and development of the digital cinema solutions of T-Systems. — Since 1994, Ruppel has been involved in various research projects and product developments in the areas of networked video solutions, digital cinema, and professional video distribution. — Ruppel holds Dr.-Ing. and Dipl.-Ing. degrees in communications engineering from Technical University of Darmstadt. He is a member of SMPTE, ITG (Informationstechnische Gesellschaft) and FKTG (Fernseh- und Kinotechnische Gesellschaft). Since 2008, he has been the chair of ITG committee 3.4 (Film Technologies).
